ai_root_cause: A physical layer issue or speed/duplex mismatch on link Fa0/2 causes excessive collisions and link instability, which repeatedly triggers Spanning Tree Topology Change Notifications (TCNs) and flushes MAC address tables.
corrected_root_cause: Redundant link without EtherChannel is causing a bridging loop / repeated STP topology changes destabilizing the network.
human_notes: A physical loop without EtherChannel was misdiagnosed as a duplex mismatch causing collisions -- a different root mechanism.

ai_root_cause: R1 is load-sharing (ECMP) default route traffic between its own WAN link and R2, or R2 is still advertising a default route into the internal routing protocol despite its WAN link being down, causing half the traffic sent to R1 (the HSRP active router) to be forwarded to R2 and dropped.
corrected_root_cause: HSRP did not fail over correctly / R2 lacks a track/preempt config, so traffic routed through R2 (whose WAN link is down) is silently dropped.
human_notes: AI proposed ECMP load-sharing / stale route advertisement; ground truth is a missing preempt config causing failed HSRP failover -- different mechanism.

ai_root_cause: VLAN 40 is missing from the VLAN database on SW2, so the switch cannot process or forward traffic for that VLAN across the trunk.

Interface Fa0/5 entered an err-disabled (Secure-shutdown) state because the laptop's MAC address violated the port security policy, which was already configured with a maximum of 1 sticky MAC address assigned to a different device.
The internal DNS server is missing its internal zone file configuration, causing internal hostname queries to time out while external queries succeed via the configured forwarder.
corrected_root_cause: Internal DNS zone is missing/not loaded on the DNS server, so internal name resolution fails while external forwarding still works.
human_notes: Root cause correct. Evidence claim said queries "time out"; actual evidence shows NXDOMAIN (non-existent domain), a different failure type than stated.

ai_root_cause: The router is load-balancing traffic to 172.16.0.0/24 across two different next hops because both the static route and OSPF route are concurrently installed in the routing table, leading to packet path oscillation across asymmetrical routes.
corrected_root_cause: Routing instability caused by two competing paths with equal/near-equal preference (equal-cost or misconfigured AD) causing route flapping/asymmetric routing.
human_notes: AI proposed static+OSPF routes both installed; ground truth is competing equal/near-equal-cost paths -- different specific mechanism despite similar shape.

ai_root_cause: The router has exhausted its NAT/PAT translation table limits (port/translation exhaustion) on the single public IP address, causing all new outbound connection attempts to be dropped.
The RADIUS server is intermittently timing out during 802.1X authentication requests, causing corporate Wi-Fi clients using WPA2-Enterprise to lose authorization and be forced to re-authenticate.

The inbound ACL on the server's VLAN interface only permits ICMP traffic from the staff subnet and lacks rules permitting TCP traffic on ports 80 (HTTP) and 443 (HTTPS), causing web traffic to be dropped by the implicit deny.
corrected_root_cause: ACL only explicitly permits ICMP and SSH (port 22) from the staff subnet; HTTP/HTTPS traffic falls through to the implicit deny at the end of the ACL.
human_notes: Root cause correct. Evidence description omitted the SSH permit line (line 20) from the 3-line ACL, describing it as a simpler 2-line ACL than it actually is.

ai_root_cause: The new switch was connected to the VTP domain in Server mode with a higher configuration revision number and a blank VLAN database (only VLAN 1), causing all other switches in the domain to overwrite their VLAN databases with its revision.
corrected_root_cause: The replacement switch had a higher VTP revision number than the rest of the domain, so it overwrote and wiped out the VLAN database network-wide when it joined.
human_notes: Root cause correct. AI stated "loss of all VLANs domain-wide" as if observed; evidence only shows two differing VTP revision numbers, not a vlan-brief confirming actual data loss.

ai_root_cause: Interface Vlan50 lacks a properly configured IPv6 address, preventing a connected IPv6 route from entering the routing table and preventing Router Advertisements from being generated.
corrected_root_cause: Router advertisements are being suppressed (ipv6 nd ra suppress) or router IPv6 forwarding is misconfigured, so SLAAC-based hosts never learn a working default gateway.
human_notes: AI blamed a missing IPv6 address on the interface; ground truth is RA (Router Advertisement) suppression -- different root mechanism.

ai_root_cause: The VLAN 60 interface (SVI) on the router is missing an 'ip helper-address' configuration, preventing DHCP broadcast requests from clients in VLAN 60 from being relayed to the centralized DHCP server in VLAN 10.

Packet fragmentation is failing because large packets (1500 bytes) exceed the GRE tunnel MTU (1476 bytes) and have the Don't Fragment (DF) bit set, causing the router to drop them when Path MTU Discovery is broken.

A bridging loop was created by connecting an unmanaged switch to two wall jacks on the same VLAN, and the lack of BPDU guard on the access ports allowed the loop to form and cause broadcast storms and frequent topology changes.

The internal DNS server is configured with a decommissioned secondary DNS server (10.10.5.6) in its forwarder list, causing a 5-10 second delay while waiting for queries to timeout before succeeding via the working path.
corrected_root_cause: Stale forwarder/secondary DNS server entry pointing to a decommissioned host is causing every query to time out against it before falling through to a working resolver.
human_notes: Root cause correct. AI added an unverified specific detail ("decommissioned last month") not present anywhere in the evidence.

ai_root_cause: An explicit 'deny tcp any any eq 1521' rule exists in the access list placed before a general permit rule, blocking the custom database port 1521 traffic while allowing ping, HTTP, and HTTPS.

IP address space overlap between the two branch offices causes routing failure; both networks use 192.168.1.0/24 internally, so the router cannot distinguish between local traffic and remote traffic for that subnet.
A native VLAN mismatch exists on the trunk link between SW1 (Native VLAN 1) and SW2 (Native VLAN 10), causing untagged traffic from VLAN 1 on one side to bleed over into VLAN 10 on the other side.
OSPF neighbor adjacency is stuck in the EXSTART/EXCHANGE state because R1 and R2 have mismatched MTU settings on their connecting interfaces.
R1 and R2 are configured with mismatched EIGRP AS numbers (R1 uses AS 100 and R2 uses AS 200), preventing them from establishing neighbor adjacencies.
The DHCP scope for VLAN 70 is exhausted (all 50 addresses are in use) because the pool size is too small to support the 60+ daily users and guest devices during peak hours.
Co-channel interference caused by an unauthorized personal Wi-Fi router operating on the same channel (channel 6) with a strong signal in the west side of the office.
The employee's device is using an outdated Wi-Fi password that was rotated last week, while other devices have been updated with the new shared WPA2-PSK.
corrected_root_cause: The employee's device still has the old, pre-rotation Wi-Fi password saved and hasn't been updated with the new shared PSK.
human_notes: Root cause is a reasonable inference but not directly evidenced -- evidence only shows repeated PSK-mismatch failures for one device, never confirms *why* (stale password vs. typo vs. wrong SSID).

ai_root_cause: The uplink interface lacks a QoS policy to prioritize voice traffic, causing VoIP packets to be dropped or delayed in the buffer (bufferbloat) when interface utilization hits 100% during large file uploads.
The device ports were incorrectly configured as community ports instead of isolated ports, allowing the devices to communicate directly with each other and bypassing the intended isolation policy.
The uplink port connecting the new switch to the main switch is configured as a static access port instead of an 802.1Q trunk, meaning traffic from VLAN 20 is not being carried beyond the new switch.

The internal DNS server serving office employees has an outdated A record for wiki.company.com pointing to the decommissioned internal server IP (10.10.9.9), while the external/VPN DNS server correctly points to the cloud-hosted IP.
The NAT ACL configured on the router is too broad ('permit ip any any'), causing internal traffic between servers on different VLANs to be unexpectedly translated instead of bypassed.
An IP address conflict is occurring on the VLAN because a manually assigned static IP address on a new PC overlaps with an active IP address (10.10.2.50) already in use by another PC.

The PC was configured with an incorrect subnet mask (/28 or 255.255.255.240 instead of /24 or 255.255.255.0), which restricts its direct local subnet communication to only IPs between 10.10.4.48 and 10.10.4.63.
corrected_root_cause: An incorrect (too narrow) subnet mask on the PC makes it think most of its own VLAN is on a different network, so it tries to route to those devices via the gateway instead of talking to them directly, and fails.
human_notes: Subnet math is correct. AI claimed the PC "can only successfully communicate" within the /28 range; only a single failed ping outside that range was shown, no successful ping inside it was captured as evidence.

ai_root_cause: Traffic from VLAN 80 to VLAN 10 is blocked by two simultaneous issues: VLAN 80 is missing from the allowed VLAN list on the trunk link between the access switch and the core switch, and the router's ACL on VLAN 80's interface explicitly permits traffic only to VLAN 20, denying VLAN 10.

VLAN 90 is failing to provide DHCP addresses because its router interface lacks an ip helper-address, and static communication to VLAN 10 fails because the router is missing a route for the VLAN 10 subnet.
The branch router's NAT overload translation table filled up during a traffic spike, and a recently added overly broad ACL is blocking legitimate return traffic for users.
corrected_root_cause: NAT/PAT table exhaustion during a traffic spike caused temporary failures, and a separately overly broad ACL (meant to block one malicious IP but matching a huge range) blocks legitimate return traffic for a subset of users even after NAT load drops.
human_notes: AI stated NAT translations were "near limit" with no stated threshold in evidence, and asserted the ACL was written for an "intended /32" (an inferred authoring intent not present in the evidence). Root cause (NAT exhaustion + overly broad ACL) is correct.

ai_root_cause: A duplex mismatch exists between the user's PC network card (configured for 100 Mbps full-duplex) and the switch port (auto-negotiated to 100 Mbps half-duplex), causing severe packet corruption evidenced by late collisions and runts.

The laptop has been statically configured with an incorrect default gateway IP address (10.10.6.99 instead of the actual router interface 10.10.6.1), preventing it from routing traffic outside of its local subnet.
